input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.

Topic: CSCI-636: Information Retrieval. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: An introduction to the theories and techniques used to construct search engines. Topics include search interfaces, traditional retrieval models (e.g., TF-IDF, BM25), modern retrieval techniques (e.g., neural reranking and retrieval), search engine evaluation, and search applications (e.g., conversational IR, enterprise search). Students will also review current IR research, provide written summaries of current research papers, and complete a group project in which they will design and execute experiments for search engine components. Prerequisites:(CSCI-603 and CSCI-605 and CSCI-661 with grades of B or better, including familiarity with computer science concepts) or CSCI-331 or equivalent courses. Students may not take and receive credit for both CSCI-636 and CSCI-536. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Spring Regeneration revision 2: use ten distinct, specific beat titles and avoid repeating any title or section label.

[scikit-learn-user-guide]
Data-analysis workflows separate data preparation, exploratory analysis, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation. Supervised methods learn mappings from examples paired with target labels, while unsupervised methods identify structure without targets. Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage. Pipelines combine transformations and estimators so the same operations are applied consistently. Cross-validation repeats training and validation across defined splits. Grouping, dimensionality reduction, classification, regression, and clustering answer different questions and require appropriate assumptions and metrics. Evaluation must match the task and the cost of errors, while distribution shift, missing data, overfitting, and unexamined sampling choices can invalidate conclusions.

beats.claim: Search engines organize documents into structured indexes that map queries to relevant records using defined data types and access paths.
beats.example: A document database stores text in tables with columns for title, content, and metadata, using primary keys to uniquely identify each record.
beats.title: Search Engine Architecture Overview
beats.visualDirection: Display a simplified block diagram showing a query input, an index lookup module, a retrieval stage, and a ranking output, with arrows indicating data flow.

beats.claim: Indexes provide additional access paths for selected workloads, enabling fast document retrieval without scanning the entire corpus.
beats.example: A term frequency index stores each unique word alongside its document IDs, allowing the system to instantly locate all documents containing a specific query term.
beats.title: Query Processing and Indexing
beats.visualDirection: Show a side-by-side comparison of a full corpus scan versus an index lookup, highlighting the reduced number of records examined in the latter.

beats.claim: Traditional retrieval models like TF-IDF and BM25 calculate relevance scores by weighing term frequency against document length and term rarity across the collection.
beats.example: In a TF-IDF calculation, the term 'machine' receives a high score in a short technical manual but a low score in a lengthy general encyclopedia article.
beats.title: Traditional Statistical Retrieval Models
beats.visualDirection: Render a bar chart comparing TF-IDF scores for a single query term across three documents of varying lengths and term frequencies.

beats.claim: BM25 refines traditional statistical approaches by incorporating position weighting and a more robust estimation of document length to improve precision.
beats.example: BM25 assigns higher relevance scores to documents where the query term appears near the beginning, reflecting stronger user intent alignment.
beats.title: BM25 Ranking Formula
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a document snippet with highlighted query terms, showing position-weighted score increments for earlier occurrences versus later ones.

beats.claim: Modern retrieval techniques employ neural reranking and retrieval models that learn complex semantic mappings between queries and documents through deep learning.
beats.example: A neural reranker takes a list of initially retrieved documents and reorders them by predicting the probability that each document satisfies the user's underlying intent.
beats.title: Modern Neural Retrieval Techniques
beats.visualDirection: Display a two-stage pipeline graphic: a fast retrieval stage followed by a neural reranking stage that outputs a refined ranked list.

beats.claim: Search engine evaluation relies on standardized metrics that measure ranking quality, relevance, and user satisfaction across test queries.
beats.example: Precision at K measures the proportion of relevant documents among the top K results, providing a direct measure of immediate query satisfaction.
beats.title: Search Engine Evaluation Metrics
beats.visualDirection: Show a table comparing Precision@10 and Recall@10 scores for three different retrieval models on a benchmark dataset.

beats.claim: Search applications extend traditional retrieval into interactive domains like conversational IR and enterprise search, adapting to dynamic user contexts.
beats.example: A conversational IR system maintains session state to resolve pronouns and follow-up questions, improving relevance across multiple turns.
beats.title: Search Applications and Conversational IR
beats.visualDirection: Present a dialogue flow diagram showing a user query, system context tracking, and an improved retrieval result for a follow-up question.

beats.claim: Data quality analysis makes missingness, duplicates, and inconsistent representation explicit, ensuring retrieval systems process reliable and clean inputs.
beats.example: Before indexing, a preprocessing step removes duplicate document entries and standardizes formatting to prevent skewed ranking results.
beats.title: Data Quality and Retrieval Integrity
beats.visualDirection: Visualize a data cleaning workflow with icons representing deduplication, normalization, and missing-value handling before the indexing stage.

beats.claim: Evaluation must match the task and the cost of errors, while distribution shift, missing data, and unexamined sampling choices can invalidate conclusions about system performance.
beats.example: A retrieval model trained on technical documents may fail on general queries due to distribution shift, requiring separate validation sets for each domain.
beats.title: Evaluation and Error Analysis
beats.visualDirection: Display a confusion matrix or error breakdown chart showing false positives and false negatives across different query types.

beats.claim: Students must apply durable concepts and problem-solving methods to design and execute experiments for search engine components, ensuring reproducible and valid results.
beats.example: A group project requires defining a baseline retrieval model, selecting a validation split, running cross-validation, and documenting how preprocessing choices affected final rankings.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: List a step-by-step checklist graphic covering experiment design, data splitting, model training, evaluation, and documentation requirements.

learningObjectives: Define and explain the core components of a search engine architecture, including indexing, retrieval, and ranking.
Compare traditional statistical retrieval models (TF-IDF, BM25) with modern neural retrieval techniques and their respective strengths.
Apply standard evaluation metrics to assess search engine performance and identify common failure modes in retrieval systems.
